chunks: "If the clock is faster than the slowest path can handle, the data doesn't arrive in time for the next edge, so flip-flops capture stale or half-settled values.
The first symptom is usually that the longest paths fail, the carry chain of an adder, say, so you get wrong results for specific data patterns while simple operations still work.
Because delay depends on temperature, voltage and the individual chip, the failure can be intermittent: it works cold and fails hot, or works on one board and not another.

Worse, if the data changes right at the sampling edge, the flip-flop can go metastable, so its output sits at an in-between level for a while and then resolves randomly, which can spread into other logic as inconsistent values and show up as crashes.
Other things go wrong too. Power and heat scale with frequency, so the chip heats up and gets slower, which can make it worse. The clock itself might not meet minimum pulse width.
And interfaces have their own limits: memory access time, flash wait states, an SPI slave's max clock.
Note that hold violations don't depend on frequency, so going faster doesn't create them.
To fix it, I'd find the failing path from timing analysis, then pipeline it, restructure the logic, raise the supply or cool the chip, or just lower the clock to what the critical path supports."
